input:
This operations case describes a defect-reduction project that was carried out on a moulding cell, and it reports the impact that the project has had on the reject rate over the course of one quarter. Before the project, the reject rate stood at 4.9%, but following the changes that were implemented, it was successfully reduced to 2.2%, which represents a substantial improvement in the performance of the cell.

In terms of volume, the cell produces 139k units per year, and at this level of output the change in the reject rate means that the operation avoids about 3753 rejected units per year, which would otherwise have been produced and subsequently scrapped. This gives a tangible sense of the scale of the benefit that the project has delivered in practice.

It is important to note, however, that the quarter in question included a planned shutdown, and the rates that are reported here are not adjusted for it. This is a relevant caveat, because the shutdown may have influenced the volumes and the production mix during the quarter, and so the reported improvement should be interpreted with this context in mind when it is compared with performance in other periods.

Going forward, it will be interesting to see whether the improved reject rate can be sustained in subsequent quarters, when the cell is operating under more normal conditions and without the disruption associated with the project itself, and the results of those quarters will provide a firmer basis on which to judge the lasting impact of the changes that have been made.
target:
A defect-reduction project on a moulding cell cut the reject rate from 4.9% to 2.2% over one quarter. At 139k units per year, the change avoids about 3753 rejected units per year.

The two figures describe the same result at different scales. The rate difference is the share of production no longer rejected; the unit figure is that difference applied to the annual volume of the cell, and it is the figure that connects the project to scrap handling, rework capacity, and material consumption. Both figures rest on the quarter's rates holding for a full year at the stated volume. The project changed the cell's reject performance within the quarter in which the changes were made; the annual unit figure is the quarter's rate difference carried forward, not a count of units observed over a year.

The quarter included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it. A shutdown changes the running hours and the mix of work the cell handled in the quarter, so the reported rates describe a quarter that was not a normal production period. The size of that effect is not separated in the reported figures, and the improvement is therefore stated as measured, with the shutdown named as part of the conditions under which it was measured.

The result is a rate, and it should be read as one. A reject rate compares rejected units with the units produced in the same period, so it is not distorted by the shutdown in the way a simple count of rejected units would be; a shorter running period produces fewer rejects and fewer good units together. The reported improvement is therefore a comparison between the cell as it ran in the project quarter and the cell as it ran in the period before the project, under production conditions that were not held constant, and it is stated without any adjustment for that difference.
